subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: Presidents Trump and Xi met on 19 November in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC (their third face-to-face encounter in 2026, after Beijing in May and Washington in September). They agreed to formulate an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship” based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, with discussion of AI governance, fentanyl, and broader cooperation. A historic first U.S.-China-Russia trilateral also occurred. Xi raised the Taiwan issue, urging the U.S. to “do the right thing” to avoid setbacks. Warm optics (including an airport embrace by Xi) contrasted with limited concrete breakthroughs; analysts note China has used the engagement window to consolidate strategic space while the U.S. has advanced new AI-chip remote-access restrictions and other controls. A fourth meeting is expected at the G20 in Miami in December, with trade-truce extension and AI/nuclear topics high on the agenda. A U.S. panel has warned that the stability narrative is masking Beijing’s continued competitive gains in technology and military domains.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The conflict that began with U.S./Israeli strikes on 28 February remains in a tense stalemate nearly nine months later. The U.S. maintains a naval blockade of Iranian ports (Task Force elements and carrier groups active); on 26–27 November U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel (M/V Pacific Archer) that allegedly attempted to breach it after warnings, with no crew casualties reported. Limited exchanges continue (Iranian targeting of U.S. radar/assets in the Gulf, U.S. responses against missile sites). Mediation via Oman and Qatar persists; Trump has signaled willingness to delay larger strikes into the new year if talks progress, while warning blockade runners will be sunk. Houthis continue attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure (Jeddah, Jazan ports, Ras Tanura refinery claims, Riyadh financial district), prompting Saudi-led coalition strikes on Houthi facilities and positions in Yemen. Israel has stated readiness to act independently if needed. Risks of escalation remain elevated around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: The war is in its 1,738th day. Ukraine has reported progress in “Operation Bear Trap,” liberating roughly 200 sq km and 14 settlements in northern Kharkiv, while Russian casualties continue at elevated levels. Ukrainian deep strikes hit Russian missile-fuel production (Tula), airfields, and oil infrastructure. Russia maintains high-tempo drone/missile attacks causing power outages and civilian casualties. Trump continues mediation efforts (including discussions with Putin in China) and has adjusted language around NATO statements; Zelensky has expressed frustration with the personal dynamic between Trump and Putin. Ukraine has offered a Black Sea ceasefire to facilitate food exports. Negotiations remain stalled on territory and security guarantees; leaked data and Ukrainian estimates point to very high cumulative Russian losses.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce (originating from earlier 2025–2026 understandings, including Busan and subsequent extensions) remains in force through approximately 10 January 2027. It includes a $30 billion reciprocal reduction framework on non-sensitive goods, Chinese suspension/extension of certain rare-earth and critical-mineral export controls (gallium, germanium, antimony, etc., further extended through late January 2027), and U.S. steps such as tariff exclusions and delayed port fees. On 25 November the USTR proposed additional tariffs (up to 20 % on many Chinese goods, with potential to reach ~40 % if the truce lapses) following a Section 301-style excess-capacity investigation covering China, the EU, and other partners. These would stack on existing duties for China. Beijing has warned of possible retaliation and called for dialogue. Effective U.S. rates on Chinese goods currently sit in the low-to-mid 20 % range under the truce; the new proposal and January deadlines introduce near-term uncertainty ahead of the Miami G20. Agricultural purchases, aircraft, and rare-earth flows remain partial or under negotiation.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent crude settled in the $90–95 range on 27 November (recent closes cited near $90.84–$95.44; WTI near $83). sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital expenditure continues at record scale (combined 2026 guidance for the largest U.S. players in the $700 billion range, with further growth projected). This is driving demand for advanced chips (TSMC concentration, HBM memory shortages), packaging, optics, power infrastructure (gas turbines with multi-year lead times, transformers, grid connections), and critical minerals/rare earths. Critical-mineral prices linked to AI infrastructure have risen substantially since late 2022. China retains dominant positions in rare-earth processing and certain magnets/materials; export-control suspensions remain temporary and aligned with the trade-truce calendar. U.S. export controls on advanced AI chips (including remote-access rules) continue. Other bottlenecks include packaging capacity, specialty gases, and power/cooling equipment. Concentration risks (Taiwan foundry, Chinese rare earths, limited turbine suppliers) create geopolitical and operational vulnerability; any disruption in Hormuz energy flows or rare-earth flows could cascade into AI build-out timelines and costs. Semiconductor capex forecasts have been revised higher on AI demand.

subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: On 19 November, Presidents Trump and Xi held their third bilateral meeting of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. They agreed to formulate an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship,” implement prior consensus, and expand cooperation on economic/trade issues, counternarcotics, AI governance/safety, and related areas. Chinese readouts described relations as “stable and positive”; Trump characterized the relationship as “very special.” A historic trilateral meeting with President Putin also occurred, producing a broadly worded “Declaration toward Peace” covering principles on conflicts including Ukraine, the Middle East, the Koreas, and Taiwan. Taiwan remained a point of friction, with Xi linking U.S. handling of the issue to overall stability and Trump reaffirming the U.S. does not support Taiwan independence. Fresh U.S. AI chip remote-access restrictions were enacted around the meeting, and no major breakthroughs on trade, rare earths, detained Americans, or Taiwan arms packages were achieved. Analysts note China has used the high-level engagement to buy time and strengthen its position while the U.S. side has secured limited concrete gains. The next leaders’ meeting is expected at the G20 in Miami in December. A U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission report warned that the unusually active engagement is masking Beijing’s continued competitive efforts.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.-Israel-Iran war (ongoing since late February) remains in a stalemate after roughly nine months. The U.S. maintains a naval blockade affecting the Strait of Hormuz; Iranian sources have reported tankers hitting mines or catching fire in the area, with suppressed shipping volumes. Iran has targeted U.S. assets in the Gulf (including radar systems in Bahrain), while the U.S. has conducted limited retaliatory strikes. President Trump has indicated he is inclined to wait until after the new year before authorizing further major strikes if no deal is reached, amid mediator talks involving Oman and Qatar and Israeli pressure for more action. Houthis continue attacks on Saudi Arabia (including missiles/drones toward Riyadh, the Eastern Province, ports, and energy infrastructure such as the Rabigh refinery), with Saudi-led coalition airstrikes in Yemen (including Hodeidah and other areas) and interceptions. Saudi Arabia has reported multiple interceptions and civilian casualties/injuries from Houthi strikes. Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb disruptions add to energy and shipping risks.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: The war is in its 1,737th day. Intense fighting continues with high daily Russian personnel losses (Ukrainian figures cite ~2,300 in recent days and cumulative losses exceeding 1.6 million). Ukraine has conducted long-range strikes on Russian airbases (e.g., damaging MiG-31s and Su-34s at Savasleyka), ships (including in Libyan and Baltic waters), and oil/refinery infrastructure. Russia has launched ballistic missiles and large drone waves against Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, causing casualties and infrastructure damage. Trump and NATO Secretary General Rutte jointly urged Russia to avoid actions that expand the war and to pursue a rapid peaceful resolution. Peace talks remain stalled, with Russian insistence on Donbas concessions as a precondition and U.S. proposals on security guarantees facing procedural delays. The U.S. approved a potential F-16 sustainment package for Ukraine; Patriot interceptor deliveries continue to face delays. North Korea has reportedly paused some military aid to Russia.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce (originating from the October 2025 Busan framework and previously extended) remains in place until 10 January 2027. It has limited additional U.S. tariff hikes and includes a Board of Trade mechanism for tariff relief on approximately $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction. On 25 November, the USTR proposed additional tariffs of up to 20% on Chinese goods (and measures on other partners) following a Section 301 excess-capacity investigation; for China these would stack on existing duties, potentially raising rates toward the upper end of the truce limits. China has opposed the move and reserved the right to respond. The Shenzhen summit produced no new tariff reductions or truce extension. China has extended certain rare-earth and critical-mineral export-control suspensions in line with the truce timeline (to roughly mid-to-late January 2027 for some measures), though core licensing requirements for several medium/heavy rare earths remain in force. Broader U.S. tariff proposals also target other Asian partners and the EU under the excess-capacity review.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance for 2026 is exceptionally large—roughly $700–725 billion across the major U.S. platforms (Amazon AWS ~$200 billion, Alphabet ~$175–185 billion, Meta ~$115–145 billion, Microsoft in a similar elevated range). This wave is crowding out conventional electronics production and stretching multiple supply chains. Critical bottlenecks include high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging capacity (TSMC advanced packaging is reported as sold out), power generation and grid interconnection, electrical equipment, and skilled labor. Rare-earth permanent magnets and related materials remain highly concentrated in China; export-control suspensions are in place under the trade truce but physical flows have not fully normalized and price premia outside China stay elevated. Copper, lithium, and other critical minerals face projected medium-term supply deficits as data-center build-out accelerates. Additional concentration risks exist in specialty materials (e.g., certain Japanese-sourced films and components) and in the power-equipment supply chain. U.S. chip-export controls continue to shape Chinese access to advanced compute. The scale of the build-out makes the AI infrastructure cycle highly sensitive to any disruption in these concentrated nodes.

sections.title: Geopolitics – Key Flashpoints

subsections.text: U.S.-China relations remain managed but tense following the November 19 Trump-Xi meeting on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen (their third in 2026). Leaders agreed to formulate an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity, with discussion of AI governance, counternarcotics, agriculture, and energy. A rare trilateral with Putin also occurred. Concrete deliverables were limited; the U.S. reaffirmed it does not support Taiwan independence while Xi linked Taiwan handling to overall stability. Fresh U.S. restrictions (effective around the meeting) blocked Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips in third-country data centers, prompting Chinese warnings of retaliation. Analysts note China has secured strategic space while the U.S. gained little new leverage; focus shifts to a possible G20 follow-up in Miami. The U.S.-Iran conflict (underway since late February 2026) continues as a grinding stalemate with naval blockade elements around the Strait of Hormuz, recurrent tanker incidents (mines, projectiles, fires), and limited exchanges of fire (U.S. strikes on Iranian sites; Iranian targeting of U.S./Gulf assets). Iran has set conditions for talks (sanctions relief, end of blockade, asset release) and rejected unconditional negotiations. Iran-backed Houthis have advanced toward Aden, consolidated near Bab el-Mandeb, and escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia (including Riyadh financial district and claimed oil infrastructure strikes), prompting intensive Saudi-led airstrikes on Houthi positions and energy/telecom sites. Displacement exceeds 360,000 since August; U.S. costs surpass $48 billion. Mediation via Oman/Qatar persists amid risks of further spillover. Ukraine-Russia fighting remains intense on day ~1,735 of the full-scale invasion. Recent days saw ~161 combat engagements, high Russian personnel losses (~1,800/day; cumulative estimates near 1.64 million), heavy drone/missile and guided bomb use, and Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and vessels (including a corvette near Benghazi and incidents in the Gulf of Finland). Putin has vowed retaliation for continued oil-plant attacks despite U.S. requests. Peace-track activity involves U.S. envoys (Kushner, Witkoff) aiming for a deal before January; Russia rejects NATO Article 5-style guarantees for Ukraine. NATO airspace incidents (Poland, others) and nuclear rhetoric continue.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance for 2026 is exceptionally large (combined Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft figures in the $700 billion range). This is crowding out other electronics production and straining the physical supply chain. Tightest bottlenecks include power generation and grid equipment (gas turbines, transformers, grid connections with multi-year lead times), rare-earth magnets and processing (China dominance; export licensing creates price divergences), advanced packaging (CoWoS and equivalents), high-bandwidth memory, and certain optical components (indium phosphide lasers). TSMC concentration in leading-edge logic, ASML in EUV, and a handful of other specialty materials (e.g., build-up film) remain structural. New U.S. rules on remote access to restricted chips and ongoing Chinese leverage over critical minerals amplify concentration risks. Physical constraints (power, minerals, packaging) are currently more binding than pure semiconductor design capacity.

subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: On 19 November, Presidents Trump and Xi held their third bilateral meeting of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Chinese readouts described the talks as “positive and constructive” and stated that the two sides agreed to map out an “action plan for a constructive relationship of strategic stability” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. They also discussed AI governance, counternarcotics, and managing differences. Xi reiterated that the U.S. should “do the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid setbacks in the relationship; Chinese statements noted Trump reaffirming the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence. The meeting occurred days after the U.S. Commerce Department issued new rules restricting Chinese remote access to advanced AI chips via overseas data centers and imposing licensing requirements on shipments to certain Southeast Asian countries. China had threatened countermeasures. Analysts note limited concrete progress beyond the existing framework, with the trade truce still set to expire on 10 January 2027. A brief trilateral encounter involving Putin also took place. U.S. panel assessments have warned that leader-level engagement is providing Beijing strategic space while competition in technology, supply chains, and military capabilities continues.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The U.S.-Iran confrontation remains active. President Trump stated he is “inclined” to resume strikes after the new year if no acceptable deal is reached, while a U.S. naval blockade of Iranian shipping continues. Iran has claimed interception of U.S. drones (including near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz) and conducted strikes on targets in Bahrain. Shipping incidents persist, with reports of tankers catching fire after hitting mines near the Strait of Hormuz. Yemen’s Houthis have escalated attacks on Saudi Arabia, claiming strikes on the Rabigh oil refinery and other targets; Saudi-led forces have intercepted missiles and drones and conducted airstrikes on Houthi infrastructure in Yemen. Gulf states have condemned Iranian actions. Diplomacy continues at a low level, but both sides maintain readiness for escalation. Risks to energy transit and regional spillover remain elevated.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: The war continues at high intensity. Russia launched large-scale drone and missile barrages (one recent overnight attack involved 186 drones, of which 161 were intercepted). Zelensky reported roughly 2,700 long-range drones, nearly 1,460 glide bombs, and 165 missiles against 20 regions over the prior week, with significant damage to infrastructure, power systems, and civilian sites (including a residential building collapse in the Kyiv region). Ukrainian forces have conducted strikes on Russian vessels (including in Libya) and domestic facilities. Ground advances by Russian forces remain incremental in the east; cumulative personnel loss estimates from Ukrainian sources remain very high. Limited spillover risks to neighboring airspace have been noted in recent days. Other developments include ongoing Houthi-Saudi exchanges and elevated tensions around energy chokepoints.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce remains in place, extended to 10 January 2027. China has suspended an additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods (retaining a 10% rate) and delayed certain port fees and other measures; corresponding U.S. suspensions (including on fentanyl-related tariffs and some Section 301 actions) continue. Discussions under the Board of Trade framework include reciprocal tariff reductions on roughly $60 billion of non-sensitive goods ($30 billion each side), though implementation details are incomplete. China is meeting some agricultural purchase targets (notably soybeans) but lagging on others; rare-earth export flows have partially recovered but remain below pre-escalation levels. The Shenzhen summit produced no new tariff extensions or major trade breakthroughs. The arrangement provides temporary stability, but both sides retain leverage and have signaled willingness to adjust measures if commitments slip. Broader U.S. tariff actions on other partners remain in the background, while technology export controls continue independently of the tariff truce.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen remains under pressure near the 160 level against the dollar, a threshold that has previously triggered intervention. Japan conducted large-scale yen purchases earlier in 2026 (including a record monthly total and limited joint action with the U.S.), and officials have issued repeated verbal warnings of readiness to act against “one-sided” moves. Finance Minister Katayama has signaled that authorities are monitoring closely and prepared for decisive steps. USD/JPY has traded in a roughly 156–160 range in recent sessions, with intervention fears capping upside at times. The Bank of Japan’s policy rate stands at 1.25% (raised in September); markets price a high probability of a further hike (to 1.50%) in December. The Federal Reserve’s target range is 3.75–4.00%, maintaining a wide rate differential that supports dollar strength. Broader central-bank trends show divergence: the Fed is expected to tighten further amid sticky U.S. inflation, the ECB is on hold with possible further hikes, and the BoJ is gradually normalizing from a still-low base. Intervention risk remains the primary near-term stabilizer for the yen, but fundamentals (rate gaps, current-account dynamics) continue to weigh.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent crude has traded in the low-to-mid $90s and WTI in the low-to-mid $80s in recent sessions, with both benchmarks posting a third consecutive weekly decline despite intraday bounces on shipping news. Key drivers include gradual recovery of flows through the Strait of Hormuz toward pre-conflict levels, rising Middle East production and alternative-route shipments, and building inventories (U.S. crude stocks rose recently). These supply factors are offsetting the geopolitical risk premium from ongoing Hormuz incidents (mines, tanker fires) and Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Short-term risks remain two-sided: further escalation (blockade-running attempts, intensified strikes, or broader regional involvement) could rapidly reprice oil higher, while sustained flow recovery and inventory builds support further downside. The EIA has projected Brent averaging around the mid-$80s next year under baseline recovery assumptions. Natural gas has been more volatile. Overall, the market is balancing a structural supply recovery narrative against persistent chokepoint vulnerability.

subsections.text: U.S. inflation remains sticky. October CPI rose 0.4% month-on-month (core +0.3%), hotter than some expectations and reinforcing concerns that progress toward 2% has stalled, particularly in services and shelter. Markets price a high probability of a December Federal Reserve hike (25 bp base case, with some discussion of a larger move); the current target range is 3.75–4.00%. Governor Waller and others have highlighted upside inflation risks. The 10-year Treasury yield has fluctuated near 5% (recently around 4.9–5.15%), with the curve reflecting both growth and policy expectations; safe-haven flows have occasionally pulled yields lower amid geopolitical headlines. The ECB has held rates (deposit facility around 2.50%) with a data-dependent stance and possible further tightening if energy effects persist. The BoJ is expected to continue gradual normalization. Bond markets are sensitive to the interplay of sticky inflation, energy prices, and geopolitical risk; higher yields raise financing costs across economies and for leveraged AI-related investment.

Ukraine has continued strikes on the Kerch Bridge, Russian oil infrastructure, and a logistics ship in the Gulf of Finland. Ground advances remain incremental; Ukraine reports localized gains in some sectors. Peace talks remain stalled. Trump described Putin as “tired” and open to a deal after APEC contacts, while Zelensky has called Putin a “killer” and expressed skepticism that pressure is sufficient. European leaders reaffirmed support.

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce (originating from the 2025 Busan framework) has been extended to January 10, 2027. It maintains reduced U.S. fentanyl-related tariffs (around 10%), suspension of certain Chinese retaliatory measures (including a 24% additional tariff layer while retaining 10%), pauses on some export controls and port fees, and ongoing talks on critical minerals, agriculture, and market access. Average effective tariffs remain elevated (U.S. on Chinese goods cited near 36.5% in earlier assessments). The November 19 Shenzhen summit produced no new tariff reductions or finalized package; discussions on reciprocal cuts covering roughly $60 billion in non-sensitive goods (including some farm products) continue but have not been implemented. Fresh U.S. AI chip restrictions (targeting remote access via Southeast Asian data centers and diversion risks) have heightened tensions and prompted Chinese warnings of countermeasures, testing the truce’s durability ahead of the January deadline. Broader Section 301 and other measures remain in place after earlier legal shifts.

subsections.title: U.S.-China / Trump-Xi
subsections.text: Presidents Trump and Xi held their third meeting of 2026 on 19 November in Shenzhen on the sidelines of APEC. Both sides described the talks as positive and constructive and agreed to develop an “action plan for a constructive strategic stability relationship” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. Xi urged the U.S. to “do the right thing” on Taiwan to avoid setbacks; Trump reiterated the longstanding U.S. position of not supporting Taiwan independence. Cooperation was discussed on AI (to keep it under human control), fentanyl/narcotics, agriculture, and energy. A subsequent trilateral session including Putin produced a joint nuclear-risk statement but little concrete progress on Ukraine or Iran. Ongoing U.S. chip-export restrictions and China’s critical-minerals leverage remain points of friction despite the diplomatic tone.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The conflict that began with U.S.-Israeli strikes in late February 2026 remains in a stalemate near day 266. Low-level exchanges continue: U.S. strikes on Iranian sites near the Strait of Hormuz (including Qeshm) and Iranian attacks/claims of mines or strikes on tankers and U.S.-linked assets in Bahrain/Kuwait. Iran asserts influence over Hormuz shipping lanes; tanker incidents have run at a high pace in November. Diplomacy via Oman/Qatar has stalled after the June memorandum. Houthis have escalated against Saudi Arabia, striking targets including Riyadh’s financial district (damaging the Public Investment Fund tower) and threatening Red Sea ports (Jeddah) and infrastructure. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted heavy strikes on Houthi positions and warned of further action; fighting in Yemen has intensified with Houthi gains in some southern areas. Trump has indicated he is “not rushing” major new strikes and could wait until after the new year. Senate efforts to constrain the war have failed.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: On the ~1,731st day of the full-scale invasion, Russia launched a major overnight barrage on 19–20 November (following Putin’s meetings in China and his vow of retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge). Ukrainian authorities reported more than 110 missiles (including ~27 ballistic) and 400+ drones; air defenses intercepted the majority. Strikes damaged three bridges across the Dnipro in Kyiv, critical infrastructure, and other sites; at least eight civilians were killed and dozens injured, with power disruptions ahead of winter. The front line remains largely static, with both sides claiming incremental gains or successful defenses in Donetsk areas. Zelenskyy has described Ukrainian positions as strong. No breakthrough on peace talks emerged from the Shenzhen trilateral. Other notes: Limited spillover (e.g., debris or drones affecting neighboring states) continues to be monitored.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce (originating from the October 2025 Busan framework and previously extended) remains in place through 10 January 2027. China’s additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods stays suspended (a 10% rate remains); the U.S. maintains reduced tariffs and suspensions on certain Section 301 measures and related actions. The 19 November Shenzhen summit produced no further extension, new reciprocal tariff cuts, or broader deal. Discussions continue on potential targeted reductions covering roughly $30 billion in non-sensitive goods on each side, agricultural purchases, and market-access issues. Critical-minerals export-control suspensions and port-fee pauses are also extended to the same January date. U.S. advanced-chip restrictions remain a live source of tension, with China having threatened countermeasures. Businesses face continued uncertainty beyond early January 2027.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen has traded in the high-159s per dollar, repeatedly testing the closely watched 160 level that has previously triggered intervention. Tokyo has issued firm verbal warnings and previously conducted large-scale yen purchases in 2026 (including a record single-session amount and some limited U.S. coordination). The BoJ policy rate remains low (around 1.0–1.25%), with a majority of economists expecting a hike (potentially to 1.50%) in December. The still-wide differential versus the Fed’s 3.75–4.00% range sustains pressure on the yen. Broader central-bank trends: the Fed is in a tightening bias after hot inflation prints; the ECB has held rates (around 2.50%) with a data-dependent stance; other banks show mixed signals amid elevated energy prices.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent crude has recently traded in the $89–92 range (closes near $89.9–91.4 in the latest sessions) and WTI near $82–84, heading for a third consecutive weekly decline of roughly 4–5% despite geopolitical noise. Key drivers include robust Middle East export flows (aided by adaptation via pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers, and tanker fleets), rising inventories in some metrics, and forecasts of a growing surplus into 2027 as shut-ins ease from earlier peaks. Risks remain elevated: near-daily Hormuz tanker incidents, Houthi threats and strikes on Saudi energy/transport targets, and the possibility of broader U.S.-Iran escalation. Short-term outlook is volatile with a residual risk premium; longer-term base cases (absent major disruption) point to easing as supply adapts, with some analysts seeing 2027 averages in the high-$80s or lower.

Energy-driven inflation and policy divergence continue to shape differentials.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance for 2026 is exceptionally large (combined figures for major U.S. players in the $700 billion range), driving intense demand for advanced chips, high-bandwidth memory, advanced packaging, power, and related materials. Bottlenecks are acute in semiconductor capacity (especially memory and packaging, with constraints expected to persist well beyond 2026), copper, rare earths, and lithium. China retains dominant processing shares for rare earths and many critical minerals. Power-grid connections, permitting, and local opposition are additional constraints. Capital availability is emerging as a limit for some players. Concentration risks across chips, packaging, rare earths, and power create vulnerability to geopolitical or trade disruptions; the boom is also crowding out capacity in other electronics segments.
